summary: TETRIS-Q is a planar-mesh tiling algorithm that combines substrate-level phonon barriers with QEC code interleaving to suppress radiation-induced correlated faults in superconducting qubits. Through over 51 million simulations on rotated surface codes, the approach achieves logical error reductions exceeding 99.8% and reduces observable transient duration by 80%, with sparse tiling enabling 87% cost reductions in barrier implementation.
motivation: Radiation events cause spatio-temporally correlated faults affecting multiple qubits on a substrate, disrupting QEC codes despite recent advances; superconducting qubits are thousands of times more sensitive to radiation than CMOS transistors, and existing solutions (underground shielding, gap engineering, quasiparticle traps) impose impractical scalability and manufacturing constraints.
method: TETRIS-Q partitions a 1741-qubit square-lattice quantum chip into tiles enclosed by phonon barriers with tunable permeability $b_p \in [0, 0.01]$, reducing quasiparticle propagation via a dampening factor $B(\Delta l) = b_p^{\Delta l}$; independently interleaved QEC codes increase physical distance between virtually close qubits; rotated surface codes (distances $d \in \{5,7,9,11\}$) are evaluated under SI1000 noise ($p = 10^{-5}$) and simulated 100 ms radiation events with $\tau_1 = 85$ µs qubits.
result: Single-qubit tiles with $b_p = 0.1$ reduce peak logical error to ~3% at distance-5 and <1% at distance-11; tiles containing up to 25% of a QEC code's qubits match single-qubit performance with >75% cost savings; interleaving four surface codes with 15-qubit tiles at $b_p = 0.1$ achieves 9.3×10⁻⁴ average logical error rate while reducing barrier cost by 70%, and combined barriers+interleaving provide up to three orders of magnitude logical error suppression.
